title: Ships of the Ancient Greeks
author: Ancient
content:
Ships of the Ancient Greeks
on the World-Wide Web

Updated: May 2, 2000

An Annotated Collection of Internet Resources:
Archaeology Sites, History Sites, Classics Sites, Museum Sites,
Bibliographies, Syllabi, Articles, Lectures, Book Reviews, and Images

This page was designed on a 15" monitor with a 640 x 480 setting.

It looks best if you visit my house and view it on my computer.

Otherwise, adjust your browser's font size setting for optimum viewing.

Ships of the Ancient Greeks - Images
A collection of 24 images from various sources
which serves as an addendum to this page.

RECENT ADDITIONS

Greek Bireme
 - Just one of several pages on this new "Encyclopedia of Ships" site, this contains an overview
of the ancient Greek bireme.  Refer to the links on the left of the page for descriptions and images of many more ancient ships.
Though the descriptions seem to have been written by a non-English speaker,  the splendid illustrations
(accessible by clicking on the small icons at the beginning of each description) make the awkward
text a minor cavil. (web site creators unknown as of  3/13/2000)

Coins of Arados - OHG 3
 - One side of a bronze coin issued by the citizen body of Arados (162/1 BC) has an image of a warship's three-pronged battering ram.
(Oliver D. Hoover, The Hoover Collection of Seleukid Coins)

The
Greek Navy
 - Two budding triearchs from British Columbia have
posted their drawings of a trireme and a bireme along with a summary of what they've
learned about shipbuilding and tactics. (Jeff N. and Jeff B., Brooke Elementary School)

Maritime Greece
 - Though concentrating
on modern Greek shipping, the site contains a stunning head-on photo of the

Olympias
 reconstruction under sail (click on the photo icon on the left side of
the page). A side view of the 
Olympias
 is displayed on the "Ships Gallery"
page, and an explanation of "why a ship is a she" is thrown in for good measure (Greek
sailors were probably telling this same joke in the 6th century B.C.).  (Paiva)

Coventry
Boatbuilders Restorations and Replicas
 - These specialists in the restoration
of vintage boats built an early test section of the 
Olympias
 for the Trireme
Trust to demonstrate the feasibility of ancient Greek construction methods. The
right-hand column of this web page also displays photos and commentary on their work
on a one third replica of the 4th century B.C. Kyrenia ship for the Manchester Museum.
(Coventry Boatbuilders & Chandlery)

Greek Cargo Ship
 -
Suspended from the ceiling of Manchester Museum's Aegean Gallery is the replica of
the 
Kyrenia
 ship built by Coventry Boatbuilders. (Manchester Museum)

Triremes
 - A
summary of trireme oar arrangement controversy. (Borimir Jordan and Alec Tilley,
Trireme Trust)

Athenian trireme diagram
 -
The most important naval vessel in the Greek world. It was about 120 feet long, 15 feet wide and
needed 170 oarsman. This cross-sectioned diagram is reproduced from Arthur Ferrill's book,

The Origins of War: From the Stone Age to Alexander the Great
. (North Park
University)

Ancient
Mediterranian Trade Map
 - A stained glass window in Northwestern University's
Wieboldt Hall. (Schaffner Library, Northwestern University)

BOOK REVIEWS AND RECOMMENDED BOOKS

Tides of War: A Novel of Alcibiades and the Peloponnesian War

by Steven Pressfield

"As a young man my grandfather served as a sail lieutenant at Sybota, Potidaea, and Scione and later in
the East as a trierarch and squadron commander at the battles of Bitch's Tomb, Abydos (for which he
was awarded the prize of valor and incidentally lost an eye and the use of his right leg), and the
Arginousai Islands."

The promise inherent in this excerpt from the first page of Steven Pressfield's TIDES OF WAR for anyone with
an interest in the ancient Greeks and their ships is
more than fulfilled in this impossible-to-put-down historical novel.  Click on this 
link to the Barnes & Noble page
, browse the reviews,
read the first chapter, and then buy this superb book.

Book Review - H. T. Wallinga, 
Ships and Sea-Power before the Great Persian War: The
Ancestry of the Ancient Trireme
 - Reviewed by Antony Graham Keen,
Department of History, University of Manchester. (
Scholia
 Review Articles, Volume 3)

Shelley Wachsmann, 
Seagoing Ships and Seamanship in the Bronze Age Levant
 - "A fascinating and intricate rendering of virtually every aspect of early sea travel - from ship construction and propulsion to war on the open water, piracy, and laws pertaining to conduct at sea."
This page on the Barnes and Noble online bookstore site includes a quote from Lionel
Casson and the book's Table of Contents.
This is a 
wonderful
 book. It is also expensive. I wish I owned a copy.
(Texas A & M University Press hardback)

Timothy T. Shaw and J. F. Coates, 
Trireme Project: Operational Experience 1987-90, Lessons Learnt
 - The account of the building and
sailing of the 
Olympias
, the famous re-construction of an ancient Greek trireme.
Those who raise eyebrows at the book's rather high price should reflect on the money
this book will save those who seek to build their own trireme.
(David Brown paperback)

Robert Gardiner and John Morrison (Editors), 
The Age of the Galley: Mediterranean Oared Vessels Since Pre-Classical Times
 - From Conway's "History of the Ship" series, this is a beautifully illustrated edition (12 x 10 inches). Chapters from "Paddled and Oared Ships Before the Iron Age" to "Naval Installations" are contributed by experts on the subjects. (U.S. Naval Institute hardcover - 30% discount)

Chester G. Starr, 
The Influence of Sea Power on Ancient History
 -
"Presented as 'an important corrective' to the work of A.T. Mahan, an American naval officer, who published two studies on the influence of seapower upon history...", Chester Starr's book has provoked its share of controversy and disagreement. The summary on the Barnes and Noble page reveals why: "
Discounting
 views of naval superiority as a major force in the development of the ancient world, this book discusses the distinct 
limitations
 of sea power from the second millennium B.C. to the end of the Roman Empire."
(Barnes and Noble hardcover)

Vincent Gabrielsen, 
The Naval Aristocracy of Hellenistic Rhodes
 -
This page on the Barnes and Noble site includes the book's Table of Contents.
I'm not familiar with this book, but the chapters "The Secrets of Rhodian Success",
"The Image-Makers", and "The Rhodian Crews" look intriguing.
(David Brow hardcover)

William L. Rodgers, 
Greek and Roman Naval Warfare: A Study of Strategy, Tactics,
and Ship Design from Salamis (480 B.C.) to Actium (31 B.C.)
 -
Exactly as the title implies, this is a wonderfully thorough examination of how naval battles of antiquity were won and lost. (U.S. Naval Institute hardcover - 30% discount)

Basil Greenhill and John Morrison, 
The Archaeology of Boats and Ships
 - Incorporates the latest research and discoveries (through 1996).
This page on the Barnes and Noble online bookstore site includes the book's Table of Contents. (U.S. Naval Institute hardcover)

Lionel Casson, 
The Ancient Mariners: Seafarers & Sea Fighters of the Mediterranean in Ancient Times
 - The updated, revised second edition (1991) of this classic work on the subject which was first published in 1959 is now available for immediate purchase on the Barnes and Noble online bookstore. (Princeton Publishing Co. paperback -  20% discount)

Also see: 
Book Review
 by Ford Weiskittel, Trireme Trust, USA. (University of Virginia)

Lionel Casson, 
Ships and Seamanship In the Ancient World
 - Lionel Casson's famed "bible for all interested in ancient ships, shipbuilding, and sailing techniques".
This page on the Barnes and Noble online bookstore site includes the book's Table of Contents. (Johns Hopkins University Press paperback)

Lionel Casson, 
Ships and Seafaring in Ancient Times
 - Another of Casson's superb books, this starts with "The Birth of the Boat" and continues through the early history of sailing vessels, warships, triremes, galleys, and merchantmen.
Table of Contents included on this Barnes and Noble page.
(University of Texas Press paperback - 20% discount)

Henry A. Ormerod, 
Piracy In the Ancient World
 - As Lionel Casson puts it: "Still the standard work on ancient piracy".  Table of Contents and a publisher's summary included on this Barnes and Noble page. (Johns Hopkins University Press paperback)

MORE ANCIENT GREEK SHIP LINKS

Greece
 - The entry for "Greece" from 
The Mariners' Museum Age of Exploration On-line Curriculum Guide
.  Though just a couple of paragraphs in length, the page is noteworthy for its coverage of two ancient Greek mariners: Scylax and Pytheas.  Included is a map of the voyage of Pytheas. (The Mariners' Museum, Newport News, Virginia)

A Lost Painting by Polygnotos at Delphi, A Reconstruction Based on the Description by Pausanius
 - Images and commentary on ancient source material used for the reconstruction. Especially relevant is the first panel of the painting: 
Menelaos' Ship
. (Glynnis Fawkes, Tufts University)

Warfare in Hellas - Naval Warfare
 - An overview of the subject including the evolution of the fighting ship, naval weapons, and sea tactics. (Martijn Moerbeek, 
Hellas:Net
)

Warfare in Hellas - The Greek Trireme
 - A couple of images and some historical background on the Battle of Salamis and the famous race to rescind the Mytilene massacre provide a good single-page overview of the topic. (Martijn Moerbeek, 
Hellas:Net
)

Trireme II
 - An updated version of Avalon Hill's classic now-out-of-print war game's rules and charts with Peloponnesian Wars historical background. (Chris Fawcett, Yankee Air Pirates)

Greek Trireme
 - Two photos of the trireme 
Olympias
, the modern reconstruction (see below) on display next to a modern Greek warship at the  port of Thessaloniki. (University of Alabama)

The Athenian Trireme

Olympias
 - 
Olympias
 is a reconstruction of an Athenian trireme
of the 5th and 4th centuries BC. Historical notes, photos, images, glossary of trireme
terms, and links to related sites all contribute to make this a web site worthy of its
subject. [The Olympias is now on permanent display at Neon Faliron, a suburb of the
port of Piraeus.] (Oxford University - Anu Dudhia for the Trireme Trust)

The Ship in the Mediterranean
 - An outline of an
excerpt from lecture notes for the course, 
History and Archeology of the Ship
.
Professor Illsley's 
complete
 lecture notes
 comprise 
the
 best source of material on the subject to be found on the World- Wide Web. (C) J.S. Illsley 1995 (University of Wales, Bangor)

History and Archaeology of the Ship
 - This is the repository of Professor Illsley's course material on the subject and is an extremely impressive example of academic use of the World-Wide Web. The syllabi, bibliographies, and lecture notes cover the period 2600 BC to the late 16th century AD. 
Hint:

Users with smaller monitors who cannot see the top frame's menu should first click on that frame and then decrease their browser's font size setting. (C) J.S. Illsley 1995- 97 (University of Wales, Bangor)

The Incarcerated Ship of Kyrenia
 - Poem by Nikos Kranidiotis on the shipwreck and reconstruction of the 4th Century B.C. sailing ship currently exhibited in the castle of Kyrenia, now under Turkish occupation.  (POSEIDON: Hellas and the Sea)

The Kyrenia Ship
 - Overview of the survey, excavation and conservation of the shipwreck and its contents. (C) J.S. Illsley 1997 (University of Wales, Bangor)

The Trireme
 - Andrew Wilson tells it like it is (was): "Thanks to her fleet of triremes - paid for with money from the silver mines - Athens could run a highly successful 'protection racket', which extorted funds from smaller states under the pretext of protecting them against the Persians". (Andrew Wilson, 
The Classics Pages
)

Ancient Galleys
 - A succinct, yet excellent, article on the Greek development of the war galley: the penteconter, the bireme, the trireme, the quadrireme, the quinquereme, and the liburne. (Stephan Schulz)

Original source text references to "trireme"
 - Over 100 hits from a search on Tufts University PERSEUS Project: Aristotle, Demosthenes, Diodorus, Herodotus, Plato, Plutarch,... They all have something to say about triremes... Also try:

Over 1000 hits from a 
search of all texts using the key word "ship"
.

Over 500 hits from a 
search of Homer using the key word "ship"
.

Perseus Encyclopedia: trireme
 - PERSEUS Encyclopedia entry with over 20 photos from the Trireme Trust. (Tufts University)

Travelling to Delphi and Olympia
 -
These pages explore the journeys of travellers to the Panhellenic sanctuaries at Delphi and Olympia.
Chapters include: 
Ships and Sea Travel
, 
Trade
, 
Colonies
 and 
Ancient Travellers
. The site seems to be "under construction" so repeat visits may turn up more material. (Maria Daniels, Tufts University)

James Joyce Speaks
 - Sound file (.au format) of James Joyce saying: "and our galleys, triremes and quadriremes, laden with all manner merchandise, furrow the waters of the known globe." (Tom Skipp and LibroNet S. L.)

STILL MORE ANCIENT GREEK SHIP LINKS

The Phoenicians: Ships and Navigation

The Western Greeks: Maritime Communications

The above two web pages are excerpted from two past exhibitions (
The Phoenicians
 and 
The Western Greeks
) at the Palazzo Grassi in Venice.  To view these two exhibitions in their
entirety, go to the 
Palazzo Grassi web site
 and scroll down the middle frame.
(
Palazzo Grassi
)

National Public Radio - Robert Ballard
 (Real Audio required)
 - NPR's Morning Edition
report on Robert Ballard's amazing discoveries in the deep waters between Sicily and Africa. Most browsers already have the Real Audio plug-in installed.
You will have to turn on your computer's speakers, though. (National Public Radio)

Underwater Archaeology: Sites Along the Mediterranean Coastline
 - All major shipwreck sites along the French Mediterranean coastline. A clickable map of the area links to details of each site and this main page includes a chronological list of wrecks ranging from Prehistory to Modern periods. A superb resource!
(
Ministry of Culture, France: Underwater Archaeology
)

The Circumnavigation of Africa
 - Polybius, Hanno, Euthymenes, and Sataspes: Vasco da Gama could only follow in their wake. (Ciaran Branigan, 
Classics Ireland
 1994 Volume 1)

Institute of Nautical Archaeology
 - Institute projects span over three thousand years of maritime history, concentrated in three primary areas: the Bronze Age Mediterranean, medieval Europe, and the colonial/early Federal New World.
(Nautical Archaeology Program, Texas A & M University)

The Bronze Age Wreck at Uluburun
 - INA article on the 11th and final expedition to excavate the Late Bronze Age shipwreck at Uluburun, near Kas in
southern Turkey. (Nautical Archaeology Program, Texas A & M University)

Underwater Archaeology of the Black Sea: Crimean Coastal Survey 1997

 - Archaeological investigations conducted along the southern coast of Ukraine reveal intensive settlement dating back more than three millennia. Extensive maps, diagrams and photographs. Chapter headings include: 
Seafaring in the Northern Black Sea: A Historical Overview
 and 
Research Goals and Methodology
. (INA and UARTC, Kiev University)

Aegean Maritime Museum in Mykonos
 - Apparently still under construction (no exhibits displayed yet, except for the ship model on the home page), this site includes a fairly detailed maritime history of the Aegean and a handy chronology.

Naval and Maritime Museums: Greece
 - Gopher sites of Greek nautical museums  - some with large image files of triremes and models of ancient ships, others with just images of museum building exteriors. (The Maritime History Virtual Archives)

Also see Ariadne's 
Maritime Museums
 WWW index.

Ancient Greek Methods of Boating and Sailing
 - A concise overview of the subject with images of a bireme, a warship, and ship construction.
[Also see an apparently 
updated version
 of this page.] (Kenny McMahon, Nick Chadha, Paul Hotchkiss)

POSEIDON:
Hellas and the Sea
 - The maritime history and mythology of Hellas and Cyprus, Hellenic maritime museums, the Greek islands, and much more...

Jason and the Argonauts
 - The definitive World-Wide Web treatment of Argonautica: myth, history, crew lists, maps,  voyage itinerary theories... Very impressive site! (POSEIDON: Hellas and the Sea)

Call for Mariners
 - The POSEIDON project's goal is to collect information about Greece and its development as a prominent maritime nation from ancient to modern times. (POSEIDON: Hellas and the Sea)

The 
Argonautica
 of Apollonius Rhodius
 - English translation of the 3rd century B.C. epic of the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts from Iolkos to the Black Sea city of Colchis -  and back again. (University of California, Berkeley: Online Medieval and Classical Library)

An Electronic Bibliography: The 
Argonautica
 of Apollonius Rhodius
 - A very well designed electronic bibliography. The organization is logical, the interface is intuitive, and the scholarship is correct.
The home page provides a link to 
Martijn Cuypers' Apollonius bibliography (1496-1997)
 at Leiden University. (Jackie Murray, University of Guelph)

Greek Naval Warfare Bibliography
 - A short, but useful, list of essential references and texts on the subject. (Trinity College)

The Battle of Salamis
 - Overview of the crucial naval battle betweeen the Greeks and the Persian Empire in 480 B.C. with links to PERSEUS references. (Thomas Martin, College of the Holy Cross)

The Battle of Syme
 - In January, 411 B.C., Spartan ships defeated a squadron of Athenian vessels off the island of Syme in the south- eastern Aegean. (Caroline L. Falkner, The Ancient History Bulletin: Vol. 9, 1995)

The Peregrinations of the Queen: Technology Transfer in the Hellenistic World
 - An un-named "monster warship", she was the pride of the fleet of King Pyrrus of Epirus after his conquest of Macedonia. (Rob S. Rice, American Philological Association Convention, 1996)

The Antikythera Mechanism
 - The discovery of an ancient Greek clockwork astronomical computer has staggering implications for current theories of ancient Greek
technology. (Rob S. Rice, USNA Eleventh Naval History Symposium, 1993)

Gears, Galleys, and Geography
 - Implications of the Antikythera mechanism, "our most exciting relic of advanced
ancient technology."  (Rob S. Rice, American Philological Association abstract, 12/29/93)

Rhodes Among the Giants: Macedon, Syria, and Rome
 - Chapter 6 of 
The Rhodian Navy
.  (Rob S. Rice, University of Pennsylvania [thesis?])

Caligula's Ship
 - Not an ancient Greek ship site, but an ancient Roman ship site. (Lake Nemi Roman Ship Reconstruction Project)
